slides.text:
You already use `%s`, `%d` and `%v`. A verb can do much more: quote a text, show a type, print a number in another base, or fill a column.

In this module you choose the right verb, shape numbers and columns, and print whole slices and maps.

Between the `%` and the verb you can add flags, a width and a precision, all optional.

The first line is pseudo code, the second is a real verb.

The verb decides how a value looks, not only its type. The same number can show as a number, as a character or in binary.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
value 65
  as a number     -> 65
  as a character  -> A
  as binary       -> 1000001

exercises.title: Quote a string
exercises.guide: Print the same text plainly and in quotes.

chunks.guide: Print a word two ways: as it is, and in quotes.

notes.text: Prints the text inside double quotes.

chunks.guide: With `%s` an empty string shows nothing. Quotes show where the text starts and ends.

exercises.title: Bools and types
exercises.guide: Print a bool, and the type of a few values.

chunks.guide: Print a bool, then its type.

notes.text: Prints a bool as true or false.
Prints the type of the value.

chunks.guide: The type follows the value: a whole number is an `int`, a decimal is a `float64`.

exercises.title: Pick the verb
exercises.guide: Print the text in quotes, then the bool, then the type of the text.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    word := "go"
    ok := true
    fmt.Printf("%___\n", word)
    fmt.Printf("%___\n", ok)
    fmt.Printf("%___\n", word)
}

exercises.title: Characters and codes
exercises.guide: Print a character, its code and its Unicode form.

chunks.guide: A rune is a number. Print it as a character, as a number and as a Unicode code.

notes.text: Prints the character the number stands for.
Prints the code point as U+ and hex digits.

chunks.guide: A plain `int` works with the character verb too.

exercises.title: Letter plus one
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `letter+1` is the code 98. With `%c` it shows as the character b, and with `%d` as the number 98.

exercises.title: Numbers in other bases
exercises.guide: Print one number in binary, octal and hexadecimal.

chunks.guide: One number, printed in three bases. Hexadecimal comes in lower and upper case.

notes.text: Binary: only 0 and 1.
Octal, base 8.
Hexadecimal, in lower case.
Hexadecimal, in upper case.

chunks.text:
n := 255
    fmt.Printf("%b %o\n", n, n)
    fmt.Printf("%x %X\n", n, n)

chunks.guide: The `#` flag adds the prefix. On text, `%x` prints the hex of every byte.

notes.text: The # flag adds the 0x prefix.
On text, prints the hex of every byte.

slides.text:
A number after the `%` sets the **width**: the least columns a value takes. A number after a dot sets the **precision**: for a float, the decimals. Flags change the padding and the sign.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
width 6, align left:
|abc   |
width 6, align right:
|   abc|

exercises.title: Decimals
exercises.guide: Print a price with the default decimals and with a set number.

chunks.guide: A float prints with six decimals by default.

notes.text: Prints a float, with six decimals.

chunks.guide: A dot and a number before the verb set the decimals. The value is rounded only in the text.

notes.text: A dot and a number set the decimals.

exercises.title: Set the decimals
exercises.guide: Print price with two decimals, then total with one decimal.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    price := 4.5
    total := 19.999
    fmt.Printf("%.___f\n", price)
    fmt.Printf("%.1___\n", total)
}

exercises.title: Pad and sign numbers
exercises.guide: Give numbers a width, and a sign.

chunks.guide: A number before the verb is the width: the least columns the value takes. It pads on the left.

notes.text: Pads with spaces on the left up to 5 columns.

chunks.guide: A `-` pads on the right. A `0` pads with zeros.

notes.text: The - flag puts the number at the left.
The 0 flag fills with zeros, not spaces.

chunks.guide: The `+` flag always shows the sign.

notes.text: The + flag shows the sign on positives too.

exercises.title: Price table
exercises.guide: Print a table with aligned columns.

chunks.guide: Two slices of the same length: the items and their prices.
Pad the name to 8 columns on the right, and the price to 6 columns with 2 decimals.

notes.text: Text pads too: with - it fills on the right.
Width 6, 2 decimals. The width comes first.

exercises.title: Where is the 7?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: The - flag pads on the right, so the 7 sits at the left of its 4 columns. Without the flag, it sits at the right.

exercises.title: Flags and width
exercises.guide: Left-align the text in 6 columns, then fill the number with zeros up to 6 columns.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    word := "go"
    n := 42
    fmt.Printf("[%___6s]\n", word)
    fmt.Printf("[%___6d]\n", n)
}

slides.text:
A verb can be applied to a whole slice or map: it is used on every element. And `Printf` never refuses a bad call. A wrong verb or a wrong count shows up as a marker inside the text.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
one verb, every element:
[a b c]  ->  ["a" "b" "c"]

bad call, no error:
text with a marker inside

exercises.title: Slices and maps
exercises.guide: One verb prints every element of a slice or a map.

chunks.guide: A slice of numbers and a slice of names.
The verb is applied to every element. `%q` quotes each name.

notes.text: The verb applies to every element of the slice.

chunks.guide: A map prints as `map[key:value]`.

notes.text: Maps print sorted by key, so the text is stable.

exercises.title: Print as Go code
exercises.guide: Print values the way you would write them in code.

chunks.guide: Declare them again.
`%#v` prints a value as Go code: with its type, its quotes and its braces.

notes.text: The # flag asks for Go code, with type and braces.

chunks.text:
fmt.Printf("%#v
", scores)
    fmt.Printf("%#v
", names)
    fmt.Printf("%#v
", stock)

exercises.title: Go code or quotes
exercises.guide: Print scores as Go code, then names as a plain list with quotes.

exercises.title: Percent and position
exercises.guide: Print a percent sign, and use an argument by its position.

chunks.guide: To print a `%` itself, write it twice.

notes.text: Two percent signs print a single one.

chunks.guide: A `[1]` after the percent picks the first argument, so one value can be used twice.

notes.text: The [1] picks the first argument by position.

chunks.guide: The position also lets you reorder the arguments.

notes.text: Takes the second argument first.

exercises.title: Format mistakes
exercises.guide: Printf does not fail on a bad call. See what it prints.

chunks.guide: A number verb on a text. The problem is printed inside the text.
A verb with no argument left.
An argument with no verb. The marker comes after the text, so `Println` adds the line break.

exercises.title: What does Print add?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: Print puts a space between two operands only when neither is a text. 30 and 31 get one, but the texts around them do not.
